```{r}
source(here::here("_defaults.R"))
library(tidyverse)
library(tidynorm)
library(scico)
library(tinytable)
library(modelsummary)
library(ggdist)
library(distributional)
library(ggarrow)
library(geomtextpath)
```

@stanleyOrderOperationsSociophonetic2022 proposes an "Order of Operations" for sociophonetic analysis.
Specifically:

1.  First, identify and label vowel class allophones.
2.  Second, identify and exclude outlier data points by speaker and by allophone.
3.  Third, normalize the data.

You can use general purpose data recoding functions (e.g. `dplyr::recode_values()` or `dplyr::replace_values()`) or the more specific [`joeyr::code_allophones()`](https://joeystanley.github.io/joeyr/reference/code_allophones.html) for the first allophone labeling step.

There are also [`joeyr::find_outliers()`](https://joeystanley.github.io/joeyr/reference/find_outliers.html) and [`joeyr::tidy_mahalanobis()`](https://joeystanley.github.io/joeyr/reference/tidy_mahalanobis.html) functions for outlier identification.
However, I've decided to also implement outlier identification functions in `{tidynorm}` v0.6.0 for a few reasons.
Firstly, if I was going to allow for filtering out data points in the normalization functions, I wanted to make outlier identification functions that matched the design of the rest of the `{tidynorm}` package.
Secondly, since `{tidynorm}` has functions for directly normalizing DCT coefficients and formant tracks, I wanted to include outlier identification functions that worked appropriately for them.

# The Identify Outlier functions

In v0.6.0, `{tidynorm}` now has three outlier identification functions

- `identify_outliers()`

- `identify_track_outliers()`

- `identify_dct_outliers()`

All three functions calculate the Mahalanobis distance for vowel tokens, and add three new columns to the input data frame

- `.mahal` : The squared Mahalanobis distance

- `.prob` : The probability of observing a Mahalanobis distance this extreme or less.

- `.outlier` : A column of logical values indicating whether or not the token exceeded the probability level specified by the user.

## Point Outliers

For point measurements, you can use `identify_outliers()`.
For the purpose of visualizing here, I'll use just the F1 and F2 dimensions to calculate the Mahalanobis Distance.

```{r}
speaker_data |> 
  identify_outliers(
    F1:F2,
    .by = c(speaker, plt_vclass),
    .level = 0.95,
    
    ## If you so wish, apply transformations 
    ## before calculating Mahalanobis D:
    # .pre_trans = hz_to_bark
  ) ->
  speaker_data_identified
```

```{r}
speaker_data_identified |> 
  select(-c(plt_vclass, ipa_vclass, vowel)) |> 
  datasummary_skim()
```

For illustration purposes, let's focus on the distributions of /æ/ for these two speakers.
First the categorical `.outlier` status.

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: plotting code
#| renderings: 
#|   - light
#|   - dark
speaker_data_identified |> 
  filter(
    plt_vclass %in% c("ae")
  ) |> 
  ggplot(
    aes(F2, F1)
  ) + 
  geom_point(
    aes(
      color = .outlier
    ),
    size = 1
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~speaker) +
  scale_x_reverse() + 
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(
    title = "/æ/ distributions"
  )

last_plot() + theme_darkmode()
```

Then, by the Mahalanobis distance

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: plotting code
#| renderings: 
#|   - light
#|   - dark
speaker_data_identified |> 
  filter(
    plt_vclass %in% c("ae")
  ) |> 
  ggplot(
    aes(F2, F1)
  ) + 
  geom_point(
    aes(
      color = sqrt(.mahal)
    ),
    size = 1
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~speaker) +
  scale_x_reverse() + 
  scale_y_reverse() +
  scale_color_binned() +
  expand_limits(
    color = 0
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "/æ/ distributions"
  )

last_plot() + 
  theme_darkmode()
```

And lastly, by `prob`.

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: plotting code
#| renderings: 
#|   - light
#|   - dark
speaker_data_identified |> 
  filter(
    plt_vclass %in% c("ae")
  ) |> 
  ggplot(
    aes(F2, F1)
  ) + 
  geom_point(
    aes(
      color = .prob
    ),
    size = 1
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~speaker) +
  scale_x_reverse() + 
  scale_y_reverse() +
  scale_color_binned(
    limits = c(0,1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "/æ/ distributions"
  )

last_plot() + 
  theme_darkmode()
```

::: callout-note
## About `.prob`

The probability of each data point is based on the chi-squared cumulative probability density function with degrees of freedom equal to the number of data dimensions.
You can compare `.mahal` from the entire data set to the relevant chi-squared distribution.

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: plotting code
#| renderings: 
#|   - light
#|   - dark
ggplot() + 
  geom_dots(
    data = speaker_data_identified,
    aes(
      .mahal,
      color = "dot",
      fill = "dot"
    ),
    shape = 19
  ) +
  stat_slab(
    aes(
      xdist = dist_chisq(df = 2),
      color = "dist"
    ),
    fill = NA,
    linewidth = 2
  ) +
  geom_text(
    x = 2.6,
    y = 0.5,
    label = "dchisq(df = 2)",
    aes(color = "dist"),
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = c(0,10)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    expand = expansion()
  ) +
  guides(color = "none", fill = "none") +
  theme_no_y()

last_plot() +
  theme_darkmode() +
  theme_no_y()
```
:::

## Track and DCT outlier detection

For outlier detection for formant tracks, first the [Discrete Cosine Transform](/posts/2025/06/2025-06-17_dct-in-tidynorm/) is applied.
Then, the Mahalanobis distance is calculated, treating each DCT coefficient for each formant as a data dimension.
For example, if you wanted to identify outliers over F1 and F2, smoothing them with 3 DCT coefficients, the Mahalanobis distance would be calculated for {F1, F2} $\times$ {0, 1, 2} = 6 dimensions.

`identify_track_outliers()` requires a `.token_id_column`.

```{r}
speaker_tracks |> 
  identify_track_outliers(
    F1:F2,
    .by = c(speaker, plt_vclass),
    .token_id_col = id,
    .time_col = t,
    .order = 3,
    .level = 0.95
  ) |> 
  reframe_with_dct_smooth(
    F1:F2,
    .by = speaker,
    .token_id_col = id,
    .time_col = t,
    .order = 3
  ) ->
  speaker_tracks_identified
```

We can look at the smoothed trajectories for /aw/ like we did the points for /æ/.

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: plotting code
#| renderings: 
#|   - light
#|   - dark
speaker_tracks_identified |> 
  filter(
    plt_vclass == "aw"
  ) |> 
  ggplot(
    aes(F2, F1)
  ) + 
  geom_arrow(
    aes(
      group = id,
      color = .outlier
    ),
    linewidth = 1,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~speaker) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(
    title = "/aw/ trajectories"
  )

last_plot() +
  theme_darkmode()
```

::: callout-note
## Weighted smooths

You could, if you found it useful, get average trajectories by getting the weighted mean of the DCT parameters, weighting them by `1 - .prob`.

```{r}
speaker_tracks |> 
  # get the .prob column
  identify_track_outliers(
    F1:F3,
    .by = c(speaker, plt_vclass),
    .token_id_col = id,
    .time_col = t,
    .order = 5,
    .level = 0.95,
    .return_dct = TRUE
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    .inv_prob = 1 - .prob
  ) |> 
  summarise(
    .by = c(speaker, plt_vclass, .param), 
    across(
      F1:F3,
      list(
        mean = \(x) mean(x, na.rm = T),
        weighted.mean = \(x) weighted.mean(x, .inv_prob, na.rm = T)
      )
    )
  ) |> 
  reframe_with_idct(
    starts_with("F"),
    .by = c(speaker, plt_vclass),
    .param_col = .param
  ) -> 
  mean_comparison
```

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: plotting code
#| renderings: 
#|   - light
#|   - dark
mean_comparison |> 
  pivot_longer(
    starts_with("F")
  ) |> 
  separate_wider_delim(
    name, 
    names = c("formant", "summary"),
    delim = "_"
  ) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = formant,
    values_from = value
  ) |> 
  filter(
    plt_vclass %in% c(
      "iy", "ey" , "ay",
      "ow"
    )
  ) |> 
  ggplot(
    aes(F2, F1)
  ) +
  geom_textpath(
    aes(
      color = summary, 
      group = interaction(plt_vclass, summary),
      label = plt_vclass
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_reverse() + 
  scale_x_reverse() +
  facet_wrap(~speaker)

last_plot() + 
  theme_darkmode()
```
:::

# The `.exclude` argument

After identifying outlier data points, you can exclude them from the normalization parameter estimation by passing `.outlier` to the `.exclude` argument in any normalization function.

```{r}
speaker_data_identified |> 
  norm_nearey(
    F1:F3,
    .by = speaker,
    .exclude = .outlier
  ) ->
  normed
```

The `.exclude` argument can actually take any expression that evaluates to `TRUE` or `FALSE`.
So, for example, you can choose a different probability level to count as an outlier like so:

```{r}
speaker_data_identified |> 
  norm_nearey(
    F1:F3,
    .by = speaker,
    .exclude = .prob > 0.8
  ) ->
  normed
```

Or, you could string together any number of logical expressions.

```{r}
speaker_data_identified |> 
  norm_nearey(
    F1:F3,
    .by = speaker,
    # exclude schwa
    .exclude = (
      .outlier & plt_vclass == "@"
    )
  ) ->
  normed
```

Combined with `.agg_by`, we can implement a version of the Watt & Fabricius normalization [@wattEvaluationTechniqueImproving2002] that's closer to the original implementation.

```{r}
speaker_data_identified |> 
  mutate(
    .by = c(speaker, plt_vclass, .outlier),
    
    # I don't want to use means from
    # low-frequency vowel classes
    n = n()
  ) |> 
  norm_generic(
    F1:F3,
    .by = speaker,
    
    # it is a by-formant method
    .by_formant = TRUE,
    
    # exclude outliers and vowel classes
    # with few tokens
    .exclude = (
      .outlier & n < 20
    ),
    
    # aggregate by vowel class
    .agg_by = plt_vclass,
    
    # scale by the mean of the formant range
    .S = mean(range(.formant, na.rm = T))
  ) ->
  normed2
```

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: plotting code
#| renderings: 
#|   - light
#|   - dark
#| crop: true
normed2 |> 
  filter(!.outlier) |> 
  ggplot(
    aes(F2_n, F1_n)
  ) + 
  geom_point(
    size = 1
  ) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  facet_wrap(~speaker) +
  coord_fixed()

last_plot() +
  theme_darkmode()
```

# Double checking your steps

Even though the outlier identification and normalization happened in two separate steps, we can still double check what we did with `check_norm()`.

```{r}
#| message: true
check_norm(
  normed2
)
```
